label: What automation buys, and what it costs

mentor.diagnosis: You treated automation as free upside. The exam tests the trade: the same property that makes it valuable is what makes it dangerous.
contrast: The same property, as a cost
Reaction time: it acts in seconds
It acts wrongly in seconds too, at full scale
One bad baseline is now on every host
Those hands also held the knowledge of how it works
Complexity and technical debt in the automation itself
That system is a single point of failure
mentor.rule: Automation multiplies whatever you give it, including mistakes. Benefits scale and so does blast radius.
mentor.tell: 'Which is a drawback of automation' expects complexity, technical debt, single point of failure, or ongoing supportability, never 'it is slower'.
mentor.trap: Every listed benefit is genuinely true, so a benefits answer always reads as correct. Check whether the stem asked for the cost.

label: Guard rails vs ticket creation vs provisioning

mentor.diagnosis: You named an automation use case that does not match what the scenario automates. Each one automates a different moment.
contrast: Creating and removing accounts from an HR trigger
'A leaver still had access three weeks later'
Standing up infrastructure to a template
Blocking a non-compliant action as it is attempted
'Engineers could create a public storage bucket'
Membership, and therefore access, from a rule
'Access is granted by job role automatically'
Raising and routing the work item
'Alerts were seen but nobody was assigned'
mentor.rule: Match the automation to the moment that failed. Access that lingered is provisioning; an action that should have been impossible is a guard rail; work nobody picked up is ticketing.
mentor.tell: Onboarding and offboarding stories are almost always user provisioning, and the exam likes the offboarding half because the risk is clearer.
mentor.trap: Guard rails and security groups both sound like preventing access. Guard rails stop an action; security groups decide membership.

label: SIEM vs SCAP vs NetFlow vs SNMP traps

mentor.diagnosis: You reached for the tool you know rather than the one that produces the data the question needs. Each of these answers a different question.
contrast: What happened across everything, correlated, with alerts
Tell you whether a host meets a configuration standard
Is this host configured to the benchmark
Watch live traffic or correlate events
Who talked to whom, how much, for how long
Exactly what was said on the wire
Scale: it is expensive to keep
A device reporting its own state change
Tell you whether one was exploited
mentor.rule: Correlation across sources is SIEM. Configuration against a standard is SCAP. Conversation metadata at scale is NetFlow. Contents is packet capture.
mentor.tell: 'Which data source identifies which internal hosts talked to the command and control address, over weeks' is NetFlow: you need metadata at volume, not payloads.
mentor.trap: A SIEM ingests all of these, so it reads as the answer to everything. The question is usually which SOURCE produces the evidence, not where you would look at it.

label: Alert tuning, alert response, and the cost of noise

mentor.diagnosis: You answered an alert quality problem with more alerting, or a containment problem with tuning. They are opposite moves.
contrast: Hundreds of alerts a day, nearly all benign
Alert tuning: raise thresholds, suppress known-good
More alerting makes the real one less likely to be seen
A confirmed malicious file on an endpoint
Tuning does nothing about a live threat
Alerts fire and nothing happens afterwards
The detection worked; the process after it did not
Fixed, but was it really fixed
Closing on the responder's word is how issues reopen
You cannot correlate what you cannot see together
mentor.rule: Tuning is a quality fix for too much noise. Quarantine is a containment action on one confirmed thing. Alert fatigue is a real failure mode and the cure is fewer, better alerts.
mentor.tell: 'Analysts have begun ignoring the alerts' is alert tuning, and it is the finding, not a complaint about the analysts.
mentor.trap: Suppressing alerts feels like hiding problems, so tuning reads as the irresponsible answer. Untuned alerting hides problems far more effectively, by burying them.

mentor.diagnosis: You named a stage of the asset lifecycle that does not match where the failure happened. The lifecycle is procurement, assignment, tracking, disposal, and each has its own failure.
contrast: Buying something that cannot meet policy
A named owner and a classification
Nobody accountable when a decision is needed
A current inventory of what exists
Defending an estate you cannot enumerate
Data destroyed, asset removed from the register
A sold laptop carrying readable company data
mentor.rule: You cannot secure, patch, or decommission an asset you do not know you own. The inventory is the control everything else depends on.
mentor.tell: 'Devices were found running unsupported software nobody knew existed' is an inventory and tracking failure, before it is a patching one.
mentor.trap: Patching is the instinctive answer to anything about out-of-date systems. You cannot patch what is not in the inventory, which is why asset management sits underneath vulnerability management.

mentor.diagnosis: You chose a disposal method that does not match whether the asset is being reused, and you may have skipped the evidence step.
contrast: The device is being redeployed, sold or returned on lease
The data is too sensitive to risk, or the media has failed
Always, when a third party did the work or an auditor will ask
mentor.rule: Reuse means sanitize. No reuse and high sensitivity means destroy. Either way, get the certificate, because without it you cannot prove it happened.
mentor.tell: 'The drives were sent to a disposal vendor' should make you look for certification. The control is not complete without evidence.
mentor.trap: Degaussing is a destruction method for magnetic media and does nothing to an SSD, which stores no magnetic domains. Media type decides which destruction method is real.

label: Application allow list vs deny list

mentor.diagnosis: You picked the list that has to enumerate everything bad. Only one of these two is possible to finish.
contrast: Allow list: high up front, stable after
Deny list: endless, and always behind
Against a zero-day or new malware
Deny list has no entry for it yet
mentor.rule: Enumerating badness is a losing game because the list is infinite and grows. Allow listing is the same logic as a firewall's implicit deny, applied to software.
mentor.tell: 'Prevent any unapproved software from executing, including software we have not seen' is an allow list. A deny list cannot make that promise.
mentor.trap: Allow listing is operationally painful, so the easier answer feels more realistic. The exam rewards the control that actually meets the stated requirement.

label: Hardening a host vs patching it

mentor.diagnosis: You answered an attack surface problem with a patch. Patching fixes known flaws in software you are running; hardening reduces how much you are running and what it exposes.
contrast: Yes: tomorrow's CVE in software you did not need
Yes: no patch fixes a default password
This is the part patching does
mentor.rule: Patching fixes what you run. Hardening reduces what you run. A fully patched host with default credentials and every service enabled is still trivially owned.
mentor.tell: 'The device cannot be patched' makes hardening and isolation the only moves left, which is also when they become compensating controls.
mentor.trap: Patching is the default answer to every vulnerability question, and it is often also correct, which trains the reflex. Read whether the flaw is a missing fix or an unnecessary exposure.
